text: Solve the question and explain it using the digrams by redrawing them

Given: Inner conductor radius: a = \sqrt{2}R, Outer conductor radius: b = 2R, Length of the coaxial cylinders: \ell, Charge on the inner conductor: Q, Outer conductor is grounded, Relative dielectric constant: \kappa = 5, The imaginary plane is parallel to the common axis and is at perpendicular distance R from the axis, Edge effects are neglected, The dielectric uniformly fills the annular region a < r < b
Find: Electric-field flux \Phi_E through the part of the longitudinal plane lying in the dielectric

1. Redraw and label the three-dimensional geometry
   Represent the setup as two coaxial cylinders of length \ell. Label the inner radius a=\sqrt{2}R, the outer radius b=2R, the free charge Q on the inner conductor, and the longitudinal plane at perpendicular distance R from the common axis. The plane is parallel to the cylinder axis, so its area element is directed in the transverse cross-section normal direction and has length element dy multiplied by dz.

2. Redraw the cross-sectional annular geometry
   x=R, x²+y²=a²=2R², x²+y²=b²=4R²
   In a cross-section perpendicular to the axis, draw concentric circles of radii \sqrt{2}R and 2R. The longitudinal plane appears as the vertical line x=R. Its intersections with the inner and outer circles determine the part of the line that lies in the dielectric annulus.

3. Determine the endpoints of the dielectric portions of the plane
   R²+y²=2R²⇒ y=± R, R²+y²=4R²⇒ y=±√(3)R
   At x=R, the inner-cylinder boundary is reached at y=\pm R, while the outer-cylinder boundary is reached at y=\pm\sqrt{3}R. Therefore, the plane intersects the dielectric in two symmetric segments: R\le y\le\sqrt{3}R and -\sqrt{3}R\le y\le-R.

4. Find the electric field in the dielectric
   mathbf D(r)=(Q)/(2π rell ) mathbf r, mathbf E(r)=(Q)/(2πvarepsilon ₀κell r) mathbf r
   Use a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length \ell within the dielectric. By cylindrical symmetry, \mathbf D is radial and constant over the curved Gaussian surface. Gauss's law gives D(2\pi r\ell)=Q, so D(r)=Q/(2\pi r\ell). Since \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\kappa\mathbf E, the electric field is \mathbf E(r)=Q\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell r).

5. Resolve the field normal to the longitudinal plane
   r=√(R²+y²), Eₓ=mathbf E·mathbf x=(Q)/(2πvarepsilon ₀κell )(R)/(R²+y²)
   Choose the plane normal as +\hat{\mathbf x}. At a point (R,y), the radial unit vector has x-component R/r. Multiplying the radial field magnitude by this component gives the normal component E_x needed in the flux integral.

6. Write the surface-flux integral over both symmetric portions
   ΦE=2ell ∫R√⁽³⁾ᴿ(Q)/(2πvarepsilon ₀κell )(R)/(R²+y²) dy
   For each strip of the plane, dA=\ell\,dy. The upper and lower dielectric segments give equal contributions because E_x depends on y^2. Hence one integral is multiplied by 2.

7. Evaluate the geometric integral
   ∫R√⁽³⁾ᴿ(R)/(R²+y²) dy= [tan ⁻¹ ((y)/(R) ) ]R√⁽³⁾ᴿ=(π)/(12)
   The required antiderivative is \tan^{-1}(y/R). At the limits, the angle difference is \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})-\tan^{-1}(1)=\pi/3-\pi/4=\pi/12. The two-segment factor has already been included in the flux expression.

8. Simplify the electric flux
   ΦE=2ell ((Q)/(2πvarepsilon ₀κell ) ) ((π)/(12) )=(Q)/(12varepsilon ₀κ)
   Cancel the cylinder length \ell and the factor of \pi. The result is independent of R and \ell because the field decreases with radius while the plane geometry supplies the corresponding angular factor.

9. Substitute the dielectric constant
   ΦE=(Q)/(12varepsilon ₀(5))=(Q)/(60varepsilon ₀)
   Using \kappa=5 gives the electric-field flux through the longitudinal plane. For Q>0 and the chosen +\hat{\mathbf x} normal, the flux is positive; changing the normal reverses its sign.

10. Distinguish electric-field flux from displacement flux and check units
   ΦD=∫mathbf D· dmathbf A=varepsilon ₀κΦE=(Q)/(12), [ΦE]=N m²/C
   The displacement flux is \Phi_D=\varepsilon_0\kappa\Phi_E, so it equals Q/12 for this surface. The requested electric-field flux is smaller by the factor \varepsilon_0\kappa in the constitutive relation. Since Q/\varepsilon_0 has units N m^2/C and \kappa is dimensionless, the final expression has the correct electric-flux units.

Answer: boxed ΦE=(Q)/(60 varepsilon ₀)
For the plane at x=R, the dielectric portions run from y=R to y=\sqrt{3}R and symmetrically from y=-\sqrt{3}R to y=-R. Gauss's law in the dielectric gives \mathbf E=Q\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell r). Integrating its component normal to the plane over both portions yields \Phi_E=Q/(12\varepsilon_0\kappa). With \kappa=5, \boxed{\Phi_E=Q/(60\varepsilon_0)}. The sign is positive for a +\hat{\mathbf x} normal and Q>0; reversing the normal reverses the sign.

operations.title: Coaxial capacitor
operations.caption: a=\sqrt{2}R,\qquad b=2R,\qquad x=R
operations.narration: We begin with a coaxial capacitor of length \ell. The inner conductor carries free charge Q, the dielectric fills the annulus, and the longitudinal plane is at distance R from the axis.

operations.title: Annular cross-section
operations.caption: x=R,\qquad x^2+y^2=2R^2,\qquad x^2+y^2=4R^2
operations.narration: Looking perpendicular to the cylinder axis reduces the setup to an annulus. The plane becomes the line x=R, and only its portions inside the annulus contribute.

operations.title: Dielectric endpoints
operations.caption: R^2+y^2=2R^2\Rightarrow y=\pm R,\qquad R^2+y^2=4R^2\Rightarrow y=\pm\sqrt{3}R
operations.narration: Substituting x=R into the circular boundaries gives y=\pm R at the inner conductor and y=\pm\sqrt{3}R at the outer conductor. Thus two symmetric segments of the plane lie in the dielectric.

operations.title: Gaussian cylinder
operations.caption: \oint\mathbf D\cdot d\mathbf A=Q,\qquad D(2\pi r\ell)=Q
operations.narration: Choose a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius r and length \ell inside the dielectric. Cylindrical symmetry makes the displacement field radial and constant over its curved surface.

operations.title: Field in dielectric
operations.caption: \mathbf D(r)=\frac{Q}{2\pi r\ell}\,\hat{\mathbf r},\qquad \mathbf E(r)=\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell r}\,\hat{\mathbf r}
operations.narration: Gauss's law gives D=Q/(2\pi r\ell). Using \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\kappa\mathbf E introduces the factor 1/(\varepsilon_0\kappa) in the electric field.

operations.title: Normal component
operations.caption: r=\sqrt{R^2+y^2},\qquad E_x=\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell}\frac{R}{R^2+y^2}
operations.narration: Flux uses the component normal to the plane, not the full radial field. At (R,y), the radial unit vector has x-component R/r, producing the stated E_x.

operations.title: Both segments
operations.caption: \Phi_E=2\ell\int_R^{\sqrt{3}R}\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell}\frac{R}{R^2+y^2}\,dy
operations.narration: A strip has area dA=\ell\,dy. The upper and lower dielectric segments contribute equally because E_x depends on y^2, so one integral is multiplied by two.

operations.title: Angular integral
operations.caption: \int_R^{\sqrt{3}R}\frac{R}{R^2+y^2}\,dy=\frac{\pi}{12}
operations.narration: The integral is an angular change in disguise. Its endpoint angles are \pi/3 and \pi/4, so the angular difference is \pi/12.

operations.title: Simplify flux
operations.caption: \Phi_E=\frac{Q}{12\varepsilon_0\kappa}
operations.narration: Substituting the angular integral cancels the cylinder length and the factor of \pi. The general electric-field flux is Q/(12\varepsilon_0\kappa).

operations.title: Insert kappa
operations.caption: \Phi_E=\frac{Q}{12\varepsilon_0(5)}=\frac{Q}{60\varepsilon_0}
operations.narration: For this dielectric, \kappa=5. With Q positive and the normal directed toward increasing x, the flux is positive.

operations.title: Flux and units
operations.caption: \Phi_D=\varepsilon_0\kappa\Phi_E=\frac{Q}{12},\qquad [\Phi_E]=\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}
operations.narration: Do not confuse electric-field flux with displacement flux. The requested quantity is \Phi_E, with units of newton metre squared per coulomb; reversing the normal reverses its sign.

operations.title: Final answer
operations.caption: \boxed{\Phi_E=\frac{Q}{60\,\varepsilon_0}
operations.narration: Therefore, for the plane at x=R and the +\hat{\mathbf x} normal, the electric-field flux is Q/(60\varepsilon_0). Reversing the normal changes the sign.
